t: The Yayoi period brought wet-rice farming to the Japanese archipelago, and with it permanent villages, stored grain, landholding and a more stratified society.

Farming migrants from the Korean Peninsula and other parts of the continent mixed with the Jōmon population, laying the foundations of the modern Japanese people and, most linguists think, spreading the Japonic languages.
Chinese histories describe the land of Wa as many scattered communities, among them the Na state, which received a golden seal in 57 CE, and Yamataikoku under Queen Himiko.
dyk: The golden seal that Emperor Guangwu of the Later Han dynasty gave to the Na state of Wo in 57 CE, recorded in the Book of the Later Han, was found in northern Kyushu in the 18th century.
ev: The earliest start for the Yayoi suggested by disputed radiocarbon dates from residue on pottery
The conventional start of the Yayoi period, as wet-rice farming spreads from northern Kyushu
Iron farming tools and weapons come into use, and large regional powers emerge across western Japan
The Na state of Wo receives a golden seal from Emperor Guangwu of the Later Han dynasty
The political entity known as Wa-koku has formed
The Wei zhi records Queen Himiko of Yamataikoku, who took the throne of Wa as a spiritual leader after a civil war
The first keyhole-shaped burial mounds mark the transition to the Kofun period
Archaeologists name the culture after the Yayoi district of Tokyo, where its pottery was first found

f.homeland: The Japanese archipelago, beginning in northern Kyushu and spreading to Honshu; Yayoi traits are strongest in Kansai and Shikoku. Key sites: Itazuke and Nabata (northern Kyushu), Yoshinogari (Saga Prefecture), Makimuku (Nara Prefecture) and the Yayoi district of Tokyo.
f.period: Conventionally c. 300 BCE – 300 CE, ending in the mid-3rd century CE with the first keyhole-shaped burial mounds; radiocarbon dates, still highly controversial, may place its start as early as c. 1000–800 BCE.
f.known: wet-rice farming in paddy fields; plain, practical pottery; bronze ceremonial bells (dōtaku), mirrors and swords; iron tools and weapons; raised-floor dwellings; moated and hilltop settlements; Queen Himiko and Yamataikoku
f.sources: Excavated settlements, paddy fields and burials; radiocarbon dating of residue on pottery; comparisons of skeletons; Chinese histories (the Book of the Later Han and the Wei zhi of the Records of the Three Kingdoms); the study of the Japonic languages.
